sections.h2: Warren County tax offices and what each one does
sections.html:
Warrenton's Administration Building on Mockingbird Lane holds both tax offices. Suite 202 is the Assessor, at 636-456-8885 extension 1227, and that staff sets the value of each parcel. Suite 200 is the Collector, at 636-456-3330, which sends the bills and receives the money.

The Collector keeps weekday hours, eight until four-thirty. Email goes to collector@warrencountymo.gov. The Collector cannot add to or change a tax statement unless the Assessor changes it first. Send questions about value to the Assessor and questions about paying to the Collector.

The Collector's site posts the 2026 rate PDF, a side by side of 2025 and 2026 rates, a tax sale list and a holiday calendar. The Assessor's site has parcel and personal property searches. Emailed assessment forms are not accepted, so use the e-file option or the mail.

The Collector mails statements during the first week of November. December 31 is the last safe day. Nothing in the mailbox by Thanksgiving means it is time to phone the office, because a lost statement does not erase the tax or any late charge.

Warren County property tax calendar
DateWhat happens
January 1Ownership on this day fixes who is taxed for the year
March 1Personal property lists go to the Assessor
First week of NovemberStatements are mailed
ThanksgivingCall the Collector if no bill has arrived
November 26 and 27, 2026Collector's office closed
December 24 and 25, 2026Collector's office closed
December 31Last postmark date to avoid penalty and interest

Between the Thanksgiving and Christmas closures, you have fewer open days than the calendar suggests. A 24 hour drop box stands to the right of the entrance.

sections.h2: How the Assessor values a house
sections.html:
Real estate is revalued every second year, in the odd-numbered ones, using values as of January 1. The latest cycle was 2025 and the next is 2027. In even years the only changes come from new construction or demolition.

Field appraisers visit every parcel, measure any added square footage and adjust depreciation on buildings. State law sets the taxed share of value at 19 percent for residences, 12 percent for farm ground and 32 percent for commercial property. A jump of more than 15 percent on a home, apart from new building, requires a physical inspection first.

Rates come from other bodies. Schools, the county, fire districts and other taxing bodies vote on theirs, and your total depends on which of them cover your address.

When a reassessment or new construction pushes a value up, the Assessor mails a Notice of Change. Measure that figure against what a buyer would really pay.

  • Step one is an informal hearing with the Assessor's staff. Carry evidence of value, such as what you paid or an appraisal.
  • Step two, if the number holds, is a Board of Equalization hearing, scheduled through the Assessor ahead of the legal cutoff.
  • The Board's ruling can go on to the State Tax Commission, which hears appeals filed within 30 days of that ruling or by the chapter's own date if later.

Complaining that taxes are high gets nowhere at a hearing, since only the house's market value is on the table. You can also pay the full current bill before delinquency, give the Collector a written protest, and sue in circuit court within 90 days. When a timely Commission appeal is pending, the disputed slice sits in a separate fund until the case ends.

The owner of record on January 1 is liable for that calendar year's tax. If you close in March, you are still the taxed owner for the year, so the settlement sheet has to say who pays the bill.

Get the parcel's balance from the Collector before closing. The counter turns away short or wrong amounts, and any delinquent year gets paid ahead of the current one, so find out about the oldest year first.

  • The office takes cash, personal checks, money orders and cashier's checks, and cards at the counter or online.
  • By phone, call the outside vendor at 1-877-690-3729 and give jurisdiction code 3563.
  • A single check may pay more than one bill.
  • Send the bottom stub of the statement along with the check.

A cash buyer can close fast, so request the payoff figure early. Tell the title company to hold back enough of your proceeds to clear every year owed. Keep the receipt with your closing file.

Moving away does not change the vehicle tax bill. Vehicles are taxed on what the owner held on January 1, even if the car was sold the next day or the owner left Missouri in June. The law has no proration.

A seller who moves soon after closing still gets that year's personal property statement, with the same December 31 postmark date. Someone arriving in Missouri on March 1, 2026 is first assessed on January 1, 2027, and pays that bill in December 2027.

sections.h2: Warren County housing at a glance
sections.html:
About 39,016 people live in Warren County, up 9.8 percent from the 2020 base. The county has 17,361 housing units, and owners live in 80.2 percent of homes. Owned homes had a median value of $260,400 in the 2020 to 2024 survey, and median rent was $995. Owners with a mortgage paid a median $1,485 a month, and those without paid $499. Builders took out 360 permits in 2025.

Warren County lies north of the Missouri River in the St. Louis metropolitan area. Interstate 70, U.S. Route 40, Route 47 and Route 94 cross it. Warrenton is the county seat. Public school districts are Warren County R-III in Warrenton and Wright City R-II. Your statement shows which district a house sits in, and that choice moves the rate.

sections.h2: Steps for a seller before listing
sections.html:
Find your latest statement and confirm the parcel number, school district and amount. Can't locate it? Call the Collector. While you are on the phone, ask whether an earlier year is still open, since it has to be paid first.

Next, look at the value. A recent Notice of Change that seems high calls for a sale price or appraisal and a request for an informal hearing. The next odd-numbered year brings a general revaluation, and buyers sometimes ask how that could move the bill. It helps to have an answer ready, even if the honest answer is that rates come from the taxing bodies.

At closing, record on the settlement sheet who pays the current year, then send the payoff and the bottom stub to the Collector. Selling for cash skips a lender's review, yet the tax rules do not bend.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Warren County property tax?
faqs.a: Go to the Collector, 101 Mockingbird Lane, Suite 200, Warrenton, or call 636-456-3330. Online, mail, the vendor phone line and the 24 hour drop box also work.

faqs.q: What is the Warren County property tax deadline?
faqs.a: December 31, by postmark. Statements arrive in the first week of November, and any older delinquent year is paid before the current one.

faqs.q: When will Warren County reassess homes again?
faqs.a: In 2027. Values reset in odd-numbered years, so 2026 changes come only from new construction or demolition.

faqs.q: Can I make a partial payment on a Warren County bill?
faqs.a: No. The Collector will not accept incorrect or partial payments, though a single check can cover several bills.

faqs.q: How do I dispute a Warren County valuation?
faqs.a: Start with an informal hearing at the Assessor's office, then a Board of Equalization appointment. Bring a sale price or appraisal, since a large tax bill is not evidence of value.
